title: Where and How Often Calcium Rises

scenes.tts: Calcium is the same ion in every cell that uses it. So the message must lie in where it rises, and when. Buffer proteins capture a free calcium ion quickly, so calcium does not travel far from its channel. A protein beside the channel sees a high level. A protein across the cell sees nothing.
scenes.visual: Cell membrane with one channel; calcium dots burst out, outer ones are captured by grey buffers; a protein beside the channel is lit, a protein across the cell stays dark.
scenes.narration: Calcium is the same ion in every cell that uses it. So the message must lie in where it rises, and when. Buffer proteins capture a free calcium ion quickly, so calcium does not travel far from its channel. A protein beside the channel sees a high level. A protein across the cell sees nothing.

scenes.tts: Under a steady stimulus, many cells do not hold calcium high. They spike again and again. In 1986, Woods, Cuthbertson and Cobbold injected single rat liver cells with a light-emitting calcium reporter. The more hormone they gave, the more often the spikes came. The dose was written in frequency, the way F M radio carries sound.

scenes.visual: A held-high plateau is crossed out; calcium spikes are drawn; a single liver cell is injected with a reporter; a low-hormone trace has few spikes and a high-hormone trace has more.

scenes.tts: Something has to count the spikes, and C a M kinase two can. Its twelve subunits are assembled around a central hub. When two neighbours hold calmodulin at the same moment, one phosphorylates the other. The phosphorylated subunit stays active after calcium falls.
scenes.caption: Something has to count the spikes, and CaM kinase II can. Its twelve subunits are assembled around a central hub. When two neighbours hold calmodulin at the same moment, one phosphorylates the other. The phosphorylated subunit stays active after calcium falls.
scenes.visual: A ring of twelve subunits around a hub; two neighbours take calmodulin, a phosphate passes from one to the other, calcium falls, and the phosphorylated subunit stays green.
scenes.narration: Something has to count the spikes, and CaM kinase II can. Its twelve subunits are assembled around a central hub. When two neighbours hold calmodulin at the same moment, one phosphorylates the other. The phosphorylated subunit stays active after calcium falls.

scenes.tts: Spikes that come close together build on each other, because subunits are still loaded from the last one. Spikes far apart each start from nothing. In 1998, De Koninck and Schulman showed with purified enzyme that the lasting activity of C a M kinase two depends on the frequency of calcium pulses. Place and timing carry the message.

scenes.visual: Two idealised panels: close spikes make the activity trace climb; far-apart spikes let it fall to nothing between each.
